To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(a) the alpine–nivality ecotone is a very narrow transition belt of about 100 m width, and (b) its position is determined by the altitude where the summer snow cover has a mean duration of 60–65 d.
the central altitude of alpine–nivil ecotone is 2967±3 m, and that the ecotone is moving upward at a rate of 0.7±0.3 m/decade.
the nival ecotone (as defined by the nivality) coincides with the summer snow profile (as defined by snow duration) and that both coincide with the summer temperature profile.

the question of how to quantify the alpine– nival ecotone.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the alpine– nival ecotone in the Alps is located right at the summer snowline and that it is moving up in altitude.
the summer snowline in the Alps has moved upwards at an average rate of about 5 m per decade since 1975.
the alpine– nival ecotone in the Alps is indeed located at the summer snowline, and the ecotone is advancing with climate change.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the summer snowline is the most important climatic boundary in the high mountains.
the alpine– nival ecotone in the Alps is located at a mean altitude of 2900 m, and the ecotone is shifting upward at a rate of 0.6 m per decade.
the summer snow profile across all Alpine climate stations is the same as the nivality profile across all Alpine plant communities, and both profiles are identical with the alpine– nival ecotone.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the summer snowline and the alpine– nival ecotone coincide, both with respect to altitude and to their temperature sensitivities, and both show a positive trend.
the summer snowline and the alpine– nival ecotone have the same altitude, which is a coincidence of the highest order.
the ecotone is not a static line but an altitude band with a width of about 100 m.
